title: Study Abroad Report: University of Pennsylvania
paragraphs: I was given the opportunity to do a four-week clerkship at the University of Pennsylvania and the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), followed by a two-week laboratory visit at the University of Texas at Southwestern and a one-week laboratory visit at Mount Sinai Hospital. This study abroad would not have been realised without the efforts of Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and the other doctors of the International Collaboration Office, 西尾-san, who respected my wish to visit laboratories in the United States in addition to the partner schools and kept adjusting the study abroad plan until just before departure, and Professor 貝淵 and Professor 尾崎, who introduced me to the laboratories. In addition, at CHOP I was greatly looked after by Dr. 西崎彰, and in NYC I also met Dr. 兼井由美子, so it was a study abroad strongly supported by doctors who graduated from Nagoya University. I would like to express my gratitude here and report on my study abroad.

The Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania is the oldest medical school in America, and it owns hospitals operated in several historic buildings in the city of Philadelphia. Also, part of the campus is the medical center district, where research institutes and hospitals are gathered. This time, I was given the opportunity to train in the pediatric ICU (PICU) of CHOP, a hospital specialised in pediatrics among them. There are several ICUs within CHOP, but the PICU is where the most severely ill children are admitted. Perhaps for that reason, I was told it is rare for students to come for a clerkship, and during the clerkship I acted together with the residents.

In the morning, I attended the lecture for residents from 7 o'clock, then rounds for the rest of the morning, a conference over lunch, chart work in the afternoon (work on one's feet until about 16:00!), and report writing at night (this was an assignment for students), so it was a very busy daily life for me, who was used to polyclinic clerkships in Japan. At first there were no students and I felt intimidated among only residents, but even if clinical methods differ, medicine is the same worldwide, and there were many things about pathophysiology that I could understand, and when I asked the people around me, they happily answered anything. What I struggled with in particular were abbreviations and brand names of drugs. Even "Dex" changed meaning with the situation, as Dextrose, Dexamethasone or Dexmedetomidine, and what was being called Atrovent sounded like atropine to me, and the residents taught me about various misunderstandings and questions that make one laugh once one gets used to them.

The ward work in the PICU was divided into four teams, and each team was assigned one attending, one fellow and two to three residents, who managed the team's patients. Attendings work in the same team for one week, fellows for two or three days, and residents for one month. The fellow changes every two or three days, and the attending changes in a week. During the four-week clerkship, I rotated through three teams. CHOP is also a research institution, and in the PICU, attendings who have research funding apparently engage in research activities other than the 12 weeks of clinical (ward) work a year. Fellows also have a research obligation of more than half a year. This way of working was very fresh to me, who was used to ward work under the primary-physician system in Japan, but there are many patients who are hospitalised in the PICU for a long time, and considering the feelings of patients, I felt it is a system that would hardly be accepted in Japan. On the other hand, handovers and chart writing were done extremely meticulously and efficiently, and the ways of communicating and using words in the medical setting were very educational.

During the four weeks of the clerkship, on weekdays I was chased by report writing until midnight every day, but on weekends I visited the area where the Amish, who continue the way of life of the time when Europeans settled, live, and visited the birthplace of Hershey's, famous for Kisses chocolate, and the clear division between on and off, in a sense a very American life, is also a good memory.

After the clerkship at CHOP, I was shown the clinical research setting at the Seaver Autism Center of Mount Sinai Hospital, where I was able to talk with many researchers involved in psychiatric clinical research, and it was a very good opportunity to think about my future, since I am interested in research in the field of psychiatry. The researchers also gather from all over the world, from Europe, Asia and South America, and the environment where people of many nationalities gather was very stimulating. Also, being able to present the research project I am working on at my university and discuss it with researchers in the same field was a very valuable experience for me. NYC is a very stimulating city no matter how many times I go, and I left NYC with the strong resolution that if I ever live in America, I will definitely live in NYC.

Finally, I moved to Texas and was looked after for two weeks in Dr. Liu's basic research laboratory at the University of Texas at Southwestern. Dr. Liu, whom I visited, also has a laboratory at the University of Tsukuba, runs laboratories in both Japan and America, and conducts research clarifying the molecular mechanisms of emotion. Although it was a short period of two weeks, I was allowed to do experiments too, and I was taught by someone who actually knows both about the differences in the systems of basic research in Japan and America, and this experience too became an opportunity to think about the future.

Before this study abroad, for various reasons the original plan was greatly changed and I was chased by preparations until the last moment, and when I boarded the departure flight I was exhausted. While feeling the local air, fitting into the place and living there, I realised once again that the understanding gained by actually getting to know various people and exchanging opinions includes things that can be explained in words and a "feeling" that cannot be explained in words. I feel that this "feeling" I sensed with my own five senses, which cannot be put into words, is what I gained from the study abroad, and I believe it will be nourishment for my future.
